Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette: Ahmed sat in his office, surrounded by the familiar trappings of a life spent in politics. Yet, despite the comfort and security that came with it, he couldn't shake off the feeling of unease that had been following him for months. It started after he gave a speech at a local veterans' gathering, where someone asked him about his time as a relief worker in a war zone. The memories came flooding back - the sounds of gunfire, the smell of burnt buildings, and the faces of those who didn't make it. As Ahmed recounted that day to himself, he couldn't help but feel the same terror he felt at the time. His mind would replay fragmented pieces of the event, like a puzzle that refused to fit together. The memories were overwhelming, making him stop whatever he was doing and retreat into his own world. These episodes had become more frequent, especially when strangers approached him or talked about military topics. He'd try to control his emotions, putting on a brave face, but inside, he was screaming. When Ahmed's assistant walked in with a concerned expression, asking if everything was okay, the unusual silence that followed made him feel like something was off. He quickly checked the doors and windows, scanning the surroundings for any signs of danger. This had become a ritual for him - every time he felt threatened, which was often. His mind would constantly scan his environment, searching for potential threats. To cope with these feelings, Ahmed threw himself into work. He'd overwork himself to keep his mind occupied, distract himself from the memories that haunted him. But even in the midst of a busy schedule, the smell of burnt coffee or toast could transport him back to those chaotic days as a relief worker. The connection was instant - the smell would trigger a memory, and he'd feel overwhelmed by emotion. Ahmed knew this wasn't healthy, but it had become his way of coping. He'd also try to distract himself with mundane tasks, like checking locks repeatedly or making lists. It was all about maintaining control, which felt precarious at best. His mind was constantly racing - "What if?" and "When will it happen again?" were the only thoughts he seemed to have space for. Despite his efforts to stay busy, Ahmed couldn't shake off the feeling that something was waiting in the shadows. The silence was oppressive, making him feel like an explosion was imminent. This sense of threat had started to creep into every aspect of his life - even conversations with strangers would leave him on edge. As a politician, Ahmed's public persona required him to be composed and confident. But behind closed doors, he felt like he was losing himself in the chaos of memories and fears. He knew he needed help, but the prospect of facing those demons head-on terrified him more than anything else. It wasn't until his daughter expressed her concern about his increasingly distant behavior that Ahmed realized something had to change. He couldn't keep living in a world where every day felt like a ticking time bomb. The thought of confronting those memories and fears was daunting, but the alternative - losing himself completely - was unthinkable.
